title: Privacy & Intellectual Property
description: What privacy means, how personal data is protected through its lifecycle, the main privacy frameworks and laws, and the four types of intellectual property.

nodes.title: Privacy
nodes.description:
"State or condition of being free from being observed or disturbed by other people." Memorize this definition for the exam.
In practice, privacy means a person can keep parts of their personal information from wider society and control what others know about them.
Misuse of personal information can harm a person, for example by limiting their job options, where they can travel, or whether they can get health insurance.

children.title: Privacy policy
children.description:
Strong privacy controls start with a good privacy policy.
The most important part of the policy is well-defined roles, with clear accountability and responsibilities.
Many regulations require a Data Controller: the owner of the privacy program, who is accountable for its controls.
The policy should state what types of personal data are collected, how the data is used and stored, how people can opt out, and which security policies protect the data.

children.title: Standards / Procedures / Baselines / Guidelines
children.description:
The documents below the privacy policy. They should be well defined and based on it:
- mandatory hardware or software mechanisms
- mandatory step-by-step instructions
- minimum security levels and mandatory configurations
- recommendations that are not mandatory

children.title: Personal Data
children.description:
The main thing privacy protects.
Information that can identify a person, either on its own or combined with other information.

children.title: PII / SPI / PHI / PI
children.description:
Abbreviations that different laws use for personal data:
- information that can identify a person
- sensitive information about a person
- information about a person's health
- information about a person, in general
Full names: Personally Identifiable Information; Sensitive Personal Information; Personal Health Information.

children.title: Direct Identifiers
children.description:
Identify a person on their own.
Examples: government ID numbers (social insurance, social security, driver's license, passport), bank account numbers, certificate numbers, names and biometric data.

children.title: Indirect Identifiers
children.description:
Do not identify a person on their own, but enough of them together can identify someone uniquely.
Examples: age, gender, ethnicity, city, state, and zip or postal code.

children.title: Online Identifiers
children.description:
Identify a person through the accounts, devices and browsers they use on the internet.
Examples: email address, IP address and cookies.

children.title: Data Lifecycle
children.description:
Every stage data passes through, from creation to destruction. Security professionals use it to choose the controls that protect data at each stage.
Classification is the most important step, done at the very start. The classification shows how valuable the data is, and sets the controls for every stage:
- where it can be stored, and with what encryption and access controls
- who can use it, and for what purposes
- who it can be shared with, and under what controls
- how long it must be kept
- how securely it must be destroyed

children.title: Creation / Update
children.description: New data is generated, or existing data is changed.

children.title: Store
children.description: Data is written to a location, such as memory or a hard drive, as soon as it is generated or changed.

children.title: Use
children.description: People or processes view or process the data, without changing it.

children.title: Share
children.description:
Data is made available to others: other parts of the organization, customers, business partners, regulators and so on.
Decide who it can be shared with, under what circumstances, and with what controls.

children.title: Archive
children.description:
Data that is no longer used actively is moved to long-term storage, to free space and reduce cost.
Keep it for as long as the data retention policy requires.

children.title: Destroy
children.description:
Data that is no longer needed is permanently destroyed, by physical or logical means.
Some data must be defensibly destroyed, depending on the requirements.

children.title: OECD Guidelines
children.description:
Privacy guidelines from an intergovernmental organization of mostly developed economies.
They are guidelines, not mandatory rules: best practice.
The most internationally recognized privacy framework, and the basis for leading privacy programs. They help an organization decide what its privacy program should cover.
They define eight principles.

children.title: Collection Limitation
children.description: Gather only the PII that is needed. Obtain it lawfully and, where appropriate, with the knowledge or consent of the data subject (the person the data is about).

children.title: Data Quality
children.description:
PII should be relevant, accurate, complete and up to date.
The organization that collects PII is accountable for its integrity and accuracy.

children.title: Purpose Specification
children.description: State why PII is being collected at the time it is collected, and be clear about how it will be used.

children.title: Use Limitation
children.description: Do not disclose or process PII for purposes other than those stated when it was collected, unless the data subject consents or the law allows it.

children.title: Security Safeguards
children.description: Protect PII with reasonable controls against loss, unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification and similar risks.

children.title: Openness
children.description:
About the organization's culture: be transparent about developments, practices and policies on PII.
Do not hide or be vague about what PII is collected and how it is used.

children.title: Individual Participation
children.description:
A data subject should be able to find out what data the controller holds about them, get a copy of it, and challenge it: have it corrected, completed or erased.
GDPR's right to erasure is often called the right to be forgotten.

children.title: Accountability
children.description:
The data controller must answer for complying with the other principles.
There must be a named owner with clear accountability for protecting PII.

children.title: GDPR
children.description:
The EU regulation at the core of EU digital privacy law, and one of the strictest privacy laws in the world.
Many countries model their privacy laws on it.
You do not need to be an expert on every privacy law for the exam.
Full name: General Data Protection Regulation.

children.title: Supervisory Authority (SA)
children.description:
GDPR requires an independent public body in each EU member state.
It monitors and enforces compliance, helps organizations become compliant, and runs investigations.
Data subjects can file complaints with it.

children.title: Breaches reported within 72 hours
children.description: The GDPR deadline for notifying the regulator of a personal data breach, counted from when the organization becomes aware of it.

children.title: Cannot Achieve Privacy without Security
children.description: Privacy depends on security controls that protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of personal data.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.description:
Legal rights given to the creators and owners of intangible assets, such as inventions, works of art, symbols and designs.
The rights give owners exclusive control over how their creations are used, distributed and sold, and let them stop others from using them without permission.
Know, at a high level, what each of the four types protects.

children.title: Trade Secret
children.description:
Confidential information that gives a business a competitive advantage.
Example: the Coca-Cola formula.
A company can take legal action against anyone who steals or discloses its trade secrets without permission.

children.title: Patent
children.description:
Gives an inventor exclusive ownership of an invention for a set period, so the inventor can profit from it. This encourages innovation.
How long a patent lasts varies widely by country. You do not need to memorize it.

children.title: Copyright
children.description:
Protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself, once it is fixed in a medium such as a book, movie or song, for a set period.
It stops others from reproducing and selling the work.
Remember: copyright protects expression.

children.title: Trademark
children.description:
Symbols, words, phrases or designs that identify a brand or product and set it apart from others.
Examples: the Nike swoosh and the McDonald's arches.
It stops others from using the same logo and confusing customers.
